title: Tacrolimus -- Continuing Education Activity
content: Tacrolimus is a medication used in the prevention and treatment of solid-organ transplant rejection and remains a cornerstone of modern immunosuppressive therapy. This activity focuses on the indications, mechanism of action, and contraindications of tacrolimus as a valuable agent in immunosuppressive therapy. The activity reviews the FDA-issued box warnings, adverse event profile, toxicity, and key considerations such as dosing, monitoring, and relevant drug interactions. Understanding the intricate pharmacology of tacrolimus empowers healthcare professionals to personalize treatment plans for individual patients. Comprehensive knowledge of tacrolimus equips healthcare professionals with a scientific foundation for the practical management of transplant immunosuppression and related conditions, supporting informed decision-making, optimized dosing regimens, and minimizing adverse reactions while maintaining therapeutic effectiveness.

title: Tacrolimus -- Indications
content: Tacrolimus is an immunosuppressant medication used to prevent organ rejection following transplantation. It is typically administered in combination with one or, most commonly, two other immunosuppressive agents. Tacrolimus also has a role in the prevention and treatment of certain autoimmune diseases.

title: Tacrolimus -- Indications -- FDA-Approved Indications
content: In solid organ transplantation, Tacrolimus is used to treat organ rejection in kidney, liver, and heart allografts. Tacrolimus is also now FDA-approved for the prevention of rejection in lung transplant patients. [1] [2] [3] Tacrolimus reduces chronic lung allograft dysfunction (CLAD). [4]

title: Tacrolimus -- Indications -- FDA-approved Indication
content: Tacrolimus is FDA-approved for short-term and noncontinuous chronic treatment of moderate to severe atopic dermatitis in nonimmunocompromised adults and children who have failed to respond adequately to other topical prescription treatments for atopic dermatitis. According to guidelines by the 2023 American Academy of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology/American College of Allergy, Asthma and Immunology, topical calcineurin inhibitors are important topical therapies for atopic dermatitis. In patients aged 3 months or older with uncontrolled atopic dermatitis refractory to moisturization alone, the panel recommends adding a topical calcineurin inhibitor such as pimecrolimus or tacrolimus. [9] [10]

title: Tacrolimus -- Mechanism of Action
content: Tacrolimus (FK 506) is a potent macrolide lactone immunosuppressive drug. Tacrolimus is a calcineurin inhibitor. It inhibits T-cell proliferation by binding to FK506 binding protein (FKBP). [16] Like cyclosporine, tacrolimus inhibits T-cell activation by blocking calcineurin. Tacrolimus binds to an intracellular protein, FKBP-12, an immunophilin structurally similar to cyclophilin. A complex forms comprising tacrolimus–FKBP-12, Ca 2+ , calmodulin, and calcineurin, leading to inhibition of calcineurin phosphatase activity. This inhibition prevents the dephosphorylation and nuclear translocation of nuclear factor of activated T-cells, thereby reducing T-cell activation. Thus, although the intracellular receptors differ, cyclosporine and tacrolimus both target the same immunosuppressive pathway. [17]

title: Tacrolimus -- Mechanism of Action -- Pharmacokinetics
content: Absorption : Tacrolimus oral bioavailability is incomplete and variable, generally ranging from 17% to 23% depending on transplant type and patient population. Immediate-release capsules require twice-daily dosing and demonstrate variable absorption influenced by food intake; high-fat meals markedly reduce peak concentrations and overall exposure. Extended-release capsules provide more consistent absorption with once-daily dosing and a longer half-life. Granule formulations used in pediatrics have slightly higher bioavailability compared to immediate-release capsules, necessitating therapeutic drug monitoring during formulation changes. Topical tacrolimus shows minimal systemic absorption, with blood concentrations often below quantifiable limits, limiting systemic exposure and toxicity risk. P-glycoprotein (P-gp/ABCB1), an efflux transporter in the gastrointestinal tract, actively pumps tacrolimus back into the intestinal lumen, limiting its absorption and contributing to interpatient variability. [18]

title: Tacrolimus -- Mechanism of Action -- Pharmacokinetics
content: Distribution : Tacrolimus is extensively bound (~99%) to plasma proteins, primarily albumin and alpha-1-acid glycoprotein, and shows high affinity for erythrocytes. [19] [20] The volume of distribution is large (~30 L/kg), reflecting widespread tissue distribution. These distribution characteristics are consistent across oral formulations. Topical tacrolimus achieves high local tissue concentrations with negligible systemic distribution.

title: Tacrolimus -- Mechanism of Action -- Pharmacokinetics
content: Metabolism : Metabolism is primarily hepatic via the CYP3A4 and CYP3A5 isoenzymes, resulting in demethylation and hydroxylation to multiple metabolites, including the major 13-demethyl tacrolimus. Some metabolites retain immunosuppressive activity. Tacrolimus also acts as a CYP3A4 inhibitor, which may contribute to clinically significant drug interactions. Metabolic pathways do not significantly differ between formulations.

title: Tacrolimus -- Mechanism of Action -- Pharmacokinetics
content: Elimination : Tacrolimus is predominantly eliminated via biliary excretion into feces (~93%), with less than 1% excreted unchanged in urine. Clearance varies with age and clinical status, averaging around 30 mL/min/kg and generally higher in pediatric populations. Half-life varies by formulation and patient characteristics: immediate-release formulations exhibit variable half-lives in adults (approximately 2.1 to 46 hours) with prolongation in hepatic impairment; extended-release formulations have a mean half-life of approximately 38 hours; pediatric patients show shorter half-lives (approximately 10 to 12 hours). Topical tacrolimus has minimal systemic clearance due to negligible systemic absorption. [21] [22] [23] [24] In summary, salient features are described below

title: Tacrolimus -- Administration -- Available Dosage Forms and Strengths
content: Tacrolimus can be administered orally, sublingually, topically, or intravenously. Oral tacrolimus is available in immediate-release and extended-release formulations (capsule and tablet). Tacrolimus is available in immediate-release capsules in 0.5 mg, 1 mg, and 5 mg strengths. Extended-release formulations include capsules in 0.5 mg, 1 mg, and 5 mg strengths, and tablets in 0.75 mg, 1 mg, and 4 mg strengths. The injectable solution is supplied at a concentration of 5 mg/mL. Additionally, granules for oral suspension are available in 0.2 mg and 1 mg packets. The various formulations have different pharmacokinetic parameters and are not interchangeable. Doses should be titrated to target trough concentrations.

title: Tacrolimus -- Administration
content: Intravenous tacrolimus use is not common due to increased nephrotoxic adverse effects. [26] [27] Tacrolimus can be administered with or without food, but may occur with food in the presence of gastrointestinal intolerance. Immediate-release doses should be 12 hours apart. Dose rounding should be to a whole number that is feasible with the available strengths. For example, IR tacrolimus comes in 0.5 mg, 1mg, and 5 mg strengths. [28] When converting from immediate-release to extended-release formulations, utilize the following factors: Immediate-release to capsule: 1 to 1 Immediate-release to tablet: 1 to 0.8 [25] [29] Sublingual-to-oral conversion rates have ranged from 1:1 to 3:1, but 1:2 has recently been the most commonly reported in studies. There has been no optimally established dosing. [30] [31]

title: Tacrolimus -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Hepatic Impairment: Tacrolimus clearance is substantially reduced in patients with severe hepatic impairment (Child-Pugh >10). These patients often exhibit higher whole-blood trough concentrations and are at increased risk for nephrotoxicity. Close therapeutic drug monitoring is essential, and dose reductions below the standard targeted range are frequently required. Posttransplant hepatic dysfunction in liver recipients may further elevate tacrolimus levels; adjust dosing based on troughs and clinical status.

title: Tacrolimus -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Renal Impairment: Although tacrolimus pharmacokinetics in renal impairment resemble those of individuals with normal renal function, clinical practice favors initiating therapy at the lower end of the therapeutic range, especially in liver or heart transplant recipients with preexisting renal dysfunction. Additional dose reductions may be required depending on trough levels and evolving renal parameters.

title: Tacrolimus -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Pregnancy Considerations: The currently available data do not suggest an increased risk of major congenital malformations following in utero exposure to tacrolimus. An increased risk of low birth weight and preterm birth was reported; however, it is probably related to the maternal condition and not to the medication. Owing to reports of hyperkalemia and renal impairment in exposed infants, renal function and potassium levels should be monitored in such newborns. [32] Disease-related risks are also elevated in pregnant transplant recipients, including higher rates of hypertension, diabetes, preeclampsia, and cholestasis of pregnancy. Maternal blood glucose and blood pressure should be closely monitored. Healthcare professionals are encouraged to advise their patients to register by contacting the Transplantation Pregnancy Registry International at 1-877-955-6877 or https://www.transplantpregnancyregistry.org

title: Tacrolimus -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Breastfeeding Considerations: Tacrolimus is present in breastmilk in trace amounts, and available evidence indicates that infant exposure is low. Clinical experience in transplant recipients has shown that breastfeeding while taking tacrolimus is acceptable. Exclusively breastfed infants may be monitored as clinically indicated. Serum tacrolimus concentrations may be measured if there is a concern for toxicity or if the infant shows unexpected symptoms. Topical tacrolimus results in minimal systemic absorption, and measured maternal blood concentrations are usually less than 2 micrograms per liter. The primary precaution is to ensure that the infant’s skin does not come into direct contact with treated areas. Current guidance allows the use of topical tacrolimus on the nipples immediately after nursing. The nipples should be gently cleaned before the next feeding. Only water miscible preparations, such as creams or gels, should be applied to the breast or nipple. Ointments should be avoided because they may expose the infant to mineral paraffins through licking. When therapy of the nipple area is needed, pimecrolimus may be preferred because it is available in water-miscible formulations. [33] The decision to breastfeed requires balancing the benefits of breastfeeding, the mother's clinical need for tacrolimus, and potential risks to the infant.

title: Tacrolimus -- Administration -- Specific Patient Populations
content: Pediatric Patients: Safety and effectiveness are established for pediatric liver, kidney, heart, and lung transplant recipients. Pediatric patients often require higher doses than adults to achieve similar trough concentrations. Evidence includes controlled and uncontrolled studies using immediate-release capsules and granules. Transplant registry data support use in pediatric lung transplantation when combined with mycophenolate mofetil or azathioprine.

content: Infection may be secondary to immunosuppression, highlighting the importance of reducing target doses while carefully monitoring to balance the risk of rejection. A meta-analysis indicates that tacrolimus probably reduces the risks of acute rejection and chronic dysfunction in lung transplant recipients, without increasing survival rates. However, it may elevate the risk of developing diabetes mellitus and renal dysfunction. These findings help guide the decision between tacrolimus and cyclosporine, weighing the benefits against potential risks. [1]

title: Tacrolimus -- Adverse Effects -- Drug-Drug Interactions
content: Mycophenolic acid (MPA): The co-administration of tacrolimus with mycophenolic acid products results in higher MPA exposure because tacrolimus does not interrupt enterohepatic recirculation the way cyclosporine does. Clinicians should monitor for MPA-associated adverse reactions and reduce the MPA dose when appropriate. Grapefruit and grapefruit juice: The concurrent administration increases tacrolimus trough concentrations and increases the risk of severe toxicities, including neurotoxicity and QT prolongation. Patients should avoid grapefruit products. Strong CYP3A inducers: The concomitant administration of strong CYP3A4 inducers such as rifampin, rifabutin, phenytoin, carbamazepine, phenobarbital, and St John’s wort significantly lowers tacrolimus concentrations, increasing the likelihood of rejection. When these agents are necessary, clinicians should increase the tacrolimus dose and closely monitor trough levels.

title: Tacrolimus -- Adverse Effects
content: Strong CYP3A inhibitors: The concomitant administration of strong CYP3A4 inhibitors, such as ritonavir and other protease inhibitors, azole antifungals such as voriconazole and posaconazole, macrolide antibiotics such as clarithromycin, nefazodone, and letermovir, markedly elevates tacrolimus concentrations, sometimes producing rapid, clinically significant peaks. Clinicians should reduce the tacrolimus dose when co-administered with voriconazole or posaconazole, and initiate early, frequent monitoring within the first several days of co-administration.

title: Tacrolimus -- Adverse Effects
content: Mild to moderate CYP3A inhibitors: Patients receiving CYP3A inhibitors, including erythromycin, fluconazole, clotrimazole, calcium channel blockers such as diltiazem and verapamil, amiodarone, danazol, ethinyl estradiol, cimetidine, and proton pump inhibitors, also increase tacrolimus levels. Clinicians should monitor trough concentrations and adjust the tacrolimus dose as needed. Other interacting drugs, such as magnesium–aluminum hydroxide antacids and metoclopramide, can increase tacrolimus exposure. Clinicians should monitor trough levels and reduce the dose when appropriate.

title: Tacrolimus -- Adverse Effects
content: Mild to moderate CYP3A inducers: The concomitant administration of Mild to moderate CYP3A inducers, such as methylprednisolone and prednisone, may decrease tacrolimus concentrations. Dose adjustments should be guided by trough level monitoring. Caspofungin decreases tacrolimus trough concentrations, and therapy should be accompanied by monitoring and titration of the tacrolimus dose. Direct-acting antiviral treatment for hepatitis C can alter tacrolimus exposure because metabolic clearance changes with improvement in hepatic function. Clinicians should closely monitor tacrolimus levels during DAA treatment and adjust dosing to maintain therapeutic exposure. Cannabidiol increases tacrolimus concentrations, requiring close monitoring and potential dose reduction to avoid toxicity.

title: Tacrolimus -- Adverse Effects
content: Caspofungin : The concomitant administration of caspofungin with tacrolimus can decrease tacrolimus whole blood trough concentrations. Monitor tacrolimus whole-blood trough concentrations and adjust the tacrolimus dose as required. [37] Magnesium and aluminum hydroxide antacids: These antacids may increase tacrolimus whole-blood trough concentrations and increase the risk of severe adverse reactions, such as neurotoxicity and QT prolongation. Clinicians should monitor tacrolimus whole blood trough concentrations and reduce the tacrolimus dose if needed. Metoclopramide : The concomitant administration of metoclopramide may increase tacrolimus whole blood trough concentrations and increase the risk of serious adverse reactions, including neurotoxicity and QT prolongation. Clinicians should monitor tacrolimus whole blood trough concentrations and adjust the tacrolimus dose downward as necessary. [38]

title: Tacrolimus -- Contraindications -- Lymphoma and other Malignancies
content: Patients receiving immunosuppressants, including tacrolimus, are at increased risk of developing lymphomas and other malignancies, particularly dermatologic malignancies. The risk appears to be related to the intensity and duration of immunosuppression rather than to any specific drug. Examine patients at increased risk for skin cancer. Limit exposure to sunlight and UV light by wearing protective clothing and applying a broad-spectrum sunscreen with a high SPF. Posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder (PTLD) has been observed in immunosuppressed organ transplant recipients. Most cases of Posttransplant lymphoproliferative disorder seem related to Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV) infection. Monitor EBV serology during treatment. [41]

title: Tacrolimus -- Contraindications -- Serious Infections
content: Bacterial, viral, fungal, and protozoal infections, including opportunistic infections. These infections may lead to serious, including fatal, outcomes. Cytomegalovirus infections: CMV-seronegative transplant recipients who receive an organ from a CMV-seropositive donor are at increased risk of developing CMV viremia and CMV disease. JC virus-associated progressive multifocal leukoencephalopathy (PML) polyomavirus-associated nephropathy, mainly caused by BK virus infection [42] [43] It is advisable to monitor for infection and adjust the immunosuppressive regimen to balance the risk of rejection with that of infection.

title: Tacrolimus -- Contraindications -- Precautions/Warnings
content: Cannabidiol : Co-administration of cannabidiol and tacrolimus may lead to higher tacrolimus blood levels, raising the risk of tacrolimus-related toxicity. Regular monitoring of tacrolimus levels and vigilance for signs of toxicity are advised. Dose adjustments of tacrolimus should be considered based on clinical judgment when used together with cannabidiol. [44] Sirolimus : Tacrolimus is not recommended for use with sirolimus. The combination of sirolimus with tacrolimus in liver transplant patients has been linked to increased mortality, graft loss, and hepatic artery thrombosis. Similarly, using sirolimus with tacrolimus in heart transplant patients is advised against due to a higher risk of insulin-dependent posttransplant diabetes mellitus, impaired renal function, and wound healing complications. Combining sirolimus with tacrolimus may also elevate the risk of thrombotic events and microangiopathy. [45]

title: Tacrolimus -- Contraindications
content: Nephrotoxicity: Tacrolimus, like other calcineurin inhibitors, can cause acute or chronic nephrotoxicity in transplant patients due to its vasoconstrictive effect on renal blood vessels, toxic tubulopathy, and tubular-interstitial effects. Acute kidney injury related to tacrolimus toxicity can lead to high serum creatinine, hyperkalemia, decreased urea secretion, and hyperuricemia, and is usually reversible. In patients with elevated serum creatinine and tacrolimus whole-blood trough levels outside the recommended range, consider reducing the dose or temporarily stopping tacrolimus. The risk of nephrotoxicity may increase when tacrolimus is given together with CYP3A inhibitors or drugs associated with nephrotoxicity (e.g., aminoglycosides, ganciclovir, amphotericin B, cisplatin, nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitors, protease inhibitors). When tacrolimus is used along with other known nephrotoxic drugs, monitor kidney function and tacrolimus blood concentrations closely, and adjust the doses of both tacrolimus and any concomitant medications accordingly. For more details, refer to drug interactions.

title: Tacrolimus -- Contraindications
content: Neurotoxicity : Tacrolimus may cause neurotoxicity. The most severe neurotoxicities include posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome (PRES), which is characterized by headache, seizures, visual disturbances, and confusion.Tacrolimus may also cause other neurologic issues, including delirium, tremor, paresthesia, altered mental state, and abnormalities in motor or sensory function. These effects often correlate with elevated tacrolimus whole blood trough levels. Clinicians should monitor for new or worsening neurologic symptoms and consider reducing the dose or discontinuing the medication if neurotoxicity is suspected. [46]

title: Tacrolimus -- Contraindications
content: Hyperkalemia : Hyperkalemia has been associated with tacrolimus use. It is essential to monitor serum potassium levels regularly. When using tacrolimus, consider the potential interactions with other medications that can cause hyperkalemia, such as potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, and angiotensin receptor blockers. Periodic testing of serum potassium should be conducted throughout the treatment. Hypertension : Hypertension is an adverse effect of tacrolimus therapy and may require antihypertensive treatment. Blood pressure control can be achieved with any of the common antihypertensive agents. However, careful consideration should be given before using agents that can cause hyperkalemia, such as potassium-sparing diuretics, ACE inhibitors, and angiotensin receptor blockers. Calcium-channel blocking drugs may increase tacrolimus blood concentrations and, therefore, require a dosage reduction of tacrolimus.

title: Tacrolimus -- Contraindications
content: QT Prolongation: Tacrolimus may prolong the QT/QTc interval and may cause Torsades de Pointes. [47] Avoid using tacrolimus in patients with congenital long QT syndrome. For patients with congestive heart failure, bradyarrhythmias, or those taking certain antiarrhythmic drugs or other medications that prolong QT, as well as individuals with electrolyte imbalances such as hypokalemia, hypocalcemia, or hypomagnesemia, consider performing electrocardiograms and regularly monitoring electrolyte levels. Immunizations : Whenever possible, administer the complete vaccine series before transplantation and before initiating tacrolimus therapy. Live vaccines should be avoided during tacrolimus treatment; this includes, but is not limited to, measles, mumps, rubella, intranasal influenza, oral polio, varicella, yellow fever, BCG, and TY21a typhoid vaccines. Inactivated vaccines deemed safe posttransplantation may not elicit a sufficient immune response during tacrolimus therapy.

title: Tacrolimus -- Contraindications
content: Myocardial Hypertrophy : Myocardial hypertrophy has been observed in infants, children, and adults, especially in those with high tacrolimus trough levels. Myocardial hypertrophy typically presents as echocardiographic concentric thickening of the left ventricular posterior wall and interventricular septum. This condition seems to be reversible in most cases after reducing the dose or discontinuing medication. [48] If myocardial hypertrophy is diagnosed, consider lowering or stopping tacrolimus.

title: Tacrolimus -- Contraindications
content: Thrombotic Microangiopathy: Cases of thrombotic microangiopathy (TMA), including hemolytic-uremic syndrome (HUS) and thrombotic thrombocytopenic purpura (TTP), have been reported in patients receiving tacrolimus. [49] Risk factors for TMA in transplant patients include, for example, severe infections, graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), HLA mismatch, and mTOR inhibitors. These factors may, either alone or in combination, increase the risk of TMA. In patients showing signs and symptoms of TMA, consider tacrolimus as a potential risk factor. The concurrent use of tacrolimus and mTOR inhibitors may also contribute to TMA risk. A high level of suspicion is necessary to identify tacrolimus-induced TMA accurately and to provide prompt, appropriate care, including discontinuation of tacrolimus and supportive measures. [50]

title: Tacrolimus -- Contraindications
content: Pure Red Cell Aplasia: Cases of pure red cell aplasia (PRCA) have been documented in patients receiving tacrolimus. The exact mechanism behind tacrolimus-induced PRCA remains unclear. Reported cases often involved patients with risk factors such as parvovirus B19 infection, underlying health conditions, or concurrent medications. If PRCA is diagnosed, it is recommended to discontinue tacrolimus. [51]

title: Tacrolimus -- Monitoring
content: Tacrolimus is a drug with a narrow therapeutic index. Therapeutic monitoring of tacrolimus in transplant patients is a valuable tool in adjusting drug levels. Since tacrolimus use is typically in combination with other immunosuppressants, target levels usually decrease as posttransplant time increases to minimize calcineurin inhibitor-mediated nephrotoxicity and adverse effects. [52] Whole-blood concentrations should be used, typically drawn within 30 minutes before the next dose. Therapeutic levels range from 5 to 20 mcg/mL, though 5 to 15 mcg/mL is often employed to alleviate toxicity while preventing rejection. [53]

title: Tacrolimus -- Monitoring
content: Additional monitoring parameters include renal function, hepatic function, serum electrolytes (Mg, Phos, K), glucose, and blood pressure. Parameters should initially be measured 2 to 3 times a week postoperatively, gradually decreasing as time passes, achieving target levels, and patient stabilization. Patients receiving intravenous tacrolimus should be monitored for signs/symptoms of hypersensitivity reactions. The intravenous formulations of both tacrolimus and cyclosporine contain polyoxyethylated castor oil. [26]

title: Tacrolimus -- Toxicity -- Signs and Symptoms of Overdose
content: Tacrolimus toxicity commonly presents as acute kidney injury. Close monitoring of serum creatinine, glomerular filtration rate, and urine output is necessary for patients on tacrolimus. Toxicity may also present as adverse effects, including tremors, electrolyte disturbances, and headaches. Monitor for neurotoxicity, nephrotoxicity, and hypertension. [54] Investigations may indicate increased serum creatinine. An electrocardiogram should be obtained to rule out QT prolongation. [47]

title: Tacrolimus -- Toxicity -- Management of Overdose
content: No specific antidote is currently available for tacrolimus toxicity, and the drug is not removed by hemodialysis. Management focuses on supportive care, including symptom monitoring and management. Consultation with the poison control center is recommended for current guidance and treatment recommendations.

title: Tacrolimus -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Management of posttransplant patients is inherently an interprofessional healthcare team effort. The combined expertise of each discipline contributes to graft longevity and improved patient quality of life. According to CMS guidelines, the minimum interprofessional transplant team includes: medical/surgical transplant clinicians, nursing, clinical transplant coordinators, social services, nutritional services, pharmacology, and financial coordination. Ensuring patients are educated and supported across medical, financial, dietary, and medication domains is essential to successful outcomes, with specialty nursing playing a key role in patient counseling.

title: Tacrolimus -- Enhancing Healthcare Team Outcomes
content: Posttransplant care involves close inpatient and outpatient follow-up. Nursing coordinates the initial administration of tacrolimus and collaborates with pharmacy staff to ensure accurate dosing. The pharmacy conducts medication reconciliation at baseline and as regimens change to prevent drug interactions. [55] Nursing also monitors for adverse effects, promptly reporting findings to the treating clinician. Clinicians integrate these observations with trough concentrations and laboratory data to guide dose adjustments. Specialty services, including transplant surgery, nephrology, hepatology, cardiology, and pulmonology, support long-term immunosuppression and graft surveillance. Neurologists evaluate tacrolimus-associated neurotoxicity, such as posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, while nephrologists assess nephrotoxicity and adjust therapy as needed. Consistent communication among nursing, pharmacy, clinicians, and the broader transplant team ensures stable tacrolimus exposure, minimizes adverse effects, and improves patient outcomes.

Neurologists evaluate tacrolimus-associated neurotoxicity, such as posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome, while nephrologists assess nephrotoxicity and adjust therapy as needed. Consistent communication among nursing, pharmacy, clinicians, and the broader transplant team ensures stable tacrolimus exposure, minimizes adverse effects, and improves patient outcomes.
